title: Who is my neighbor? (Luke 10:25–37)
hookLine: a lawyer's question and a story that asks who acted like a neighbor

cards: It starts as a test. A lawyer, an expert in the law of Moses, stands up: "Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?" Jesus turns it back: how do you read the law?

The lawyer answers well, joining two lines from Deuteronomy and Leviticus: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength, and with all thy mind; and thy neighbour as thyself."
Jesus says: "This do, and thou shalt live." But the lawyer, wanting to justify himself, asks one more question, about where the edges are.

teach.h: WHO IS MY NEIGHBOR? WHERE DO I STOP?
teach.b: "And who is my neighbour?" Where can I stop? Jesus answers with a story.
"A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead."

teach.h: A PRIEST, A LEVITE: THE OTHER SIDE.
teach.b: A priest passes by on the other side. Then a Levite, a temple worker, does the same. Readers have guessed why, fear, hurry, worry about touching what might be a corpse, but Luke is silent.

Then a Samaritan comes, one of the same people whose village, a chapter ago, would not receive Jesus. "And when he saw him, he had compassion on him," the same words Luke used for Jesus at the widow's gate in Nain.
He bandages the wounds, pouring in oil and wine, puts the man on his own animal and walks.
He leaves two coins, two pence in the King James, with the innkeeper: "Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee."

Then Jesus flips the question: "Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves?" The lawyer doesn't say the word Samaritan; some readers think he couldn't bring himself to.
He says: "He that shewed mercy on him." And Jesus: "Go, and do thou likewise." The lawyer wanted a boundary.

teach.h: NOT WHO IS, BUT WHO WAS A NEIGHBOR.
teach.b: Neighbor isn't a category of people you owe.

how: Hospitals, charities and the emergency-helper laws known as Good Samaritan laws take their name from this story.

o: the one near you, your neighbor
a stranger traveling the same road
a friend who has done you a favor

p: passed by on the other side

games.q: you're a Samaritan on the Jericho road. a man from the other side of an old feud lies beaten and half dead. what do you do?
o: pass by on the other side.
bandage him, put him on your animal, and pay for the inn.
go and report it in the next town.
games.why: the Samaritan has compassion, cares for him himself, and promises to pay whatever more it costs.

practice: Think about your own road, the commute, the hallway at work, the group chat, and who has been left out, knocked down by bad news, or stuck beside it.

Then think of someone from the other side of some line, politics, faith, class, a family feud, hold them in mind without arguing, and picture crossing the road toward them as the Samaritan did, with one small act of mercy.
If you pray, hold that person before God; if you don't, simply picture the crossing.

wordCard.voice: Plesion, the Greek word behind neighbor, meaning the one near you: a lawyer's question, and Jesus' story of a Samaritan who stops on the road, turning the question into who acted as a neighbor.

orig.note: Greek: near, nearby, the one near you. the word behind "neighbor."

carryVoice: Your line: go and do likewise. Mercy crossed the road. That's day five hundred forty-one.
